advisory.overview: Zod schema-validation library through 4.6.5 contains an uncontrolled resource consumption vulnerability that allows attackers to exhaust memory by submitting a large array to an application using an array schema without a length constraint. Attackers can exploit the handleArrayResult parse logic in $ZodArray, which accumulates every validation issue for each failing element with no cap or early termination, causing the process to allocate excessive issue objects and crash due to out-of-memory conditions.
advisory.title: Zod can exhaust memory while validating oversized constrained collections

advisory.overview:
### Summary

follow-redirects 1.16.0 and 1.16.1 validate the documented sensitiveHeaders option with instanceof Array. An array created in another JavaScript realm is silently replaced with an empty list, so a caller-declared custom credential header can be forwarded to an attacker-controlled cross-origin redirect destination.

### Details

Affected versions

The sensitiveHeaders option was introduced in 1.16.0. Published 1.16.0 and 1.16.1 both reproduced, giving a tested affected range of 1.16.0 through 1.16.1. The source checkout was pinned at revision 46301256333c90b7faac7aa126effe72ec16d16e; the exact npm 1.16.1 artifact reproduced independently.

Root cause

index.js resets options.sensitiveHeaders when its local isArray() helper returns false. That helper uses value instanceof Array, which depends on realm identity. The same file already uses Array.isArray(options.headers), which correctly recognizes arrays across realms.

Suggested remediation

Use Array.isArray(value) for sensitiveHeaders, then validate and normalize each member as a header-name string. Add same-realm and node:vm cross-realm tests for cross-origin redirects, including the array-form headers representation. Verify that custom sensitive names are removed while unrelated headers remain unchanged.

Duplicate review

The public advisory history contains other sensitive-header findings, including array-form headers and regular-expression handling, but focused repository searches found no report describing cross-realm validation as of 2026-10-25. A private or differently worded report may already exist.

### Proof of concept

Start two loopback HTTP servers. The first returns a 302 redirect to the second. Send X-API-Key and list that name in sensitiveHeaders, then compare a normal array with a genuine cross-realm array created by:

```js
const vm = require('node:vm');
const sensitiveHeaders = vm.runInNewContext(`['X-API-Key']`);
```

Observed against both source and the exact npm 1.16.1 package:

- Same-realm ['X-API-Key']: the redirect target did not receive the key.
- Cross-realm ['X-API-Key']: Array.isArray(value) was true, value instanceof Array was false, and the redirect target received X-API-Key.
- An unrelated X-Harmless header remained present in both cases.

The complete 3.5 KB loopback-only harness and raw JSON output are available privately.

### Impact

custom credential disclosure. Exploitation requires a direct caller or wrapper that preserves a cross-realm sensitiveHeaders array, a custom credential listed in that option, and an attacker-controlled or compromised endpoint that returns a cross-origin redirect. The directly demonstrated result is disclosure of the custom header value, potentially exposing an API key or service token until revocation.

Built-in Authorization, Proxy-Authorization, and Cookie protections remained effective. Exact Axios 1.20.0 with follow-redirects 1.16.1 did not reproduce because Axios normalized the array; this report does not claim that Axios is affected. No third-party service was tested.
advisory.title: follow-redirects: Cross-realm sensitiveHeaders arrays are discarded and custom credentials can follow redirects

advisory.overview:
### Summary

`launch-editor` checked `fs.existsSync(fileName)` before passing a supplied path to an editor command. On Windows, an attacker can bypass this check with a crafted path ending in `\\..:line:column`. This removes the requirement that the attacker be able to place a file with a malicious filename.

Combined with the `%` escaping issue described in [GHSA-698v-4r3x-3vcv](https://github.com/vitejs/launch-editor/security/advisories/GHSA-698v-4r3x-3vcv), this bypass can lead to OS command injection when an attacker controls the file argument.

### Impact

Only apps that runs on Windows is affected.

### Details

The earlier advisory assumed that `fs.existsSync()` required an attacker-controlled filename to exist. This advisory covers a bypass of that requirement.

A crafted value ending in `\\..:1:1` is interpreted differently by `launch-editor-middleware`, `launch-editor`, and Windows:

1. `launch-editor-middleware` calls `path.resolve()` while the final path component is `..:1:1`, so it is not treated as a parent-directory component.
2. `launch-editor` treats `:1:1` as a line-and-column suffix and removes it, leaving a path ending in `\\..`.
3. On Windows, `fs.existsSync()` accepts the resulting path as the existing parent directory even though the attacker-controlled preceding component does not exist.
4. Because the existence check passes, the crafted filename reaches the Windows shell command.
advisory.title: launch-editor: `fs.existsSync()` existence check can be bypassed on Windows

advisory.overview:
### Impact

A single request can crash any application using `body-parser` with default options. When a request carries a `Content-Encoding` (for example `gzip`), `body-parser` pipes it into a decompression stream and, after reading the body, leaves that stream piped with no error listener. A payload of one valid compressed frame followed by trailing bytes decodes and the application responds normally, but the trailing bytes then reach the already-finished decoder, which emits an error that is re-thrown as an uncaught exception and terminates the process. No authentication or matching route is required, since parsing runs before routing.

### Patches

Fixed in body-parser 2.4.0 and 1.20.9. Upgrade to one of these versions.

### Workarounds

Pass `inflate: false` to the body-parser middleware if the application does not need to accept compressed request bodies. This rejects encoded requests before any decompression stream is created.
advisory.title: body-parser vulnerable to Denial of Service via trailing bytes after a compressed request body

advisory.title: SVGO removeScripts plugin leaves some executable scripts intact

advisory.overview:
## Summary

SVGO's opt-in `removeScripts` plugin failed to remove some executable links. Namespace-prefixed SVG anchors and URL schemes containing ASCII tabs or newlines could bypass its checks. Applications that used this plugin as their only protection for untrusted SVG input could expose users to cross-site scripting (XSS).

SVGO is an optimizer rather than a comprehensive sanitization library, but `removeScripts` is maintained for consumers that already rely on it to remove common script execution paths.

## Details

Two related bypasses were present:

1. The plugin inspected unprefixed SVG `<a>` elements but did not recognize namespace-prefixed SVG anchors such as `<svg:a>` when the prefix was bound to the SVG namespace. Their executable `href` or namespaced `*:href` values remained intact.
2. The URL check did not account for ASCII tab, line-feed, or carriage-return characters embedded in a scheme. Browsers remove these characters before parsing the scheme, so values such as `java	script:` could remain executable after bypassing the plugin's `javascript:` check.

Anchors in unrelated custom namespaces are not executable SVG anchors and remain untouched.

## Impact

If an application optimized attacker-controlled SVGs with `removeScripts` and then served the result in an active browser context, a victim could follow a link that executes script in the SVG's origin. Depending on the embedding and origin configuration, this could expose cookies or local storage, modify content, or perform actions as the victim.

The plugin is opt-in, so consumers that do not enable it are not relying on the affected behavior. Typical local optimization of trusted SVG files is not affected.

## Patches

Upgrade to one of the following releases for the maintained release line in use:

| Release line | Patched version | Plugin |
| --- | --- | --- |
| v2 | 2.8.4 | `removeScriptElement` |
| v3 | 3.3.5 | `removeScriptElement` |
| v4 | 4.1.0 | `removeScripts` |

The fix makes SVG anchor handling namespace-aware and strips ASCII tabs, line feeds, and carriage returns before checking executable URL schemes.

SVGO v1 is no longer maintained. Users of v1 should upgrade to a supported release line.

## Workarounds

For hostile input, use a dedicated SVG sanitization tool before passing the SVG to SVGO. Applications can also reject links from untrusted SVG input and avoid serving user-controlled SVGs in an active same-origin context.

## References

- v4 fix: https://github.com/svg/svgo/pull/2268
- related executable URL hardening: https://github.com/svg/svgo/pull/2263
- v3 backport: https://github.com/svg/svgo/pull/2269
- v2 backport: https://github.com/svg/svgo/pull/2272
- v4.1.0 release: https://github.com/svg/svgo/releases/tag/v4.1.0
- v3.3.5 release: https://github.com/svg/svgo/releases/tag/v3.3.5
- v2.8.4 release: https://github.com/svg/svgo/releases/tag/v2.8.4
advisory.title: SVGO: removeScripts allows executable links through namespace and control-character bypasses
